title: "Local AI Websites: your first source search"
format: html
filters:
  - kai-prince-sfhea/local-ai-websites
---

This tutorial uses ordinary QMD and YAML. Start with source search, then change
one display label and compare two meanings of a word. No model, API token or
author-written JavaScript is needed.

## 1. Render and preview this page

Install the extension following its
[README](https://github.com/kai-prince-sfhea/local-ai-websites#install-from-github),
then copy this `example.qmd` into your consumer folder. Its front matter already
activates the GitHub-installed filter; use the README's unqualified selector for
a local installation.

Use your editor's Render/Preview controls, or run from that folder:

```sh
quarto render example.qmd
quarto preview example.qmd
```

Use the served HTTP preview, rather than opening the HTML with `file://`. You
should see this tutorial, the source excerpts below and a **Search** control.

## 2. Search one source

The following fenced Div is both ordinary page content and a selected source.
Its native ID is `math-group-action`; its display label is **Mathematics: group
action**.

::: {#math-group-action .local-ai-source data-source-label="Mathematics: group action"}
### Group action

A group action assigns a transformation to each group element. The identity
acts as the identity transformation, and composition respects multiplication.
This definition concerns algebra, not an educational research method.
:::

In the panel below, enter `#math-group-action` and select **Search**. You should
get one exact-ID result, **Mathematics: group action**. Follow its link to return
to the source above. Source links identify material to read; they do not certify
its truth or replace its qualifications.

::: {.local-ai}
### Try source search

Enter a term or source identity. Read the original source for context.
:::

## 3. Change a display label

In this QMD's source, find the source Div opening line and change only its label:

```markdown
::: {#math-group-action .local-ai-source data-source-label="Algebra: group action"}
```

Keep its existing content and closing fence. Render again, refresh the preview
and search `#math-group-action` again. The result is now **Algebra: group action**;
the stable source ID and link still point to the same excerpt. You can change
visible wording without changing the concept's source identity.

## 4. Compare meanings without conflating them

Now search for `action`. Both the mathematics excerpt and the education excerpt
below can match that word. Lexical search returns possible sources; it does not
assert that their meanings are equivalent. The distinct labels and destinations
let you choose the relevant context. Search `#education-action-research` to
select the education source exactly.

::: {#education-action-research .local-ai-source data-source-label="Education: action research"}
### Action research

Action research is an inquiry approach in which practitioners investigate and
reflect on changes to their practice. It does not assert a group action.
:::

::: {#evidence .local-ai-source data-source-label="Evidence and generated proposals"}
### Evidence and review

A generated proposal is unreviewed. A source reference identifies material to
inspect; it does not prove that the material supports every generated claim.
An absence of search results does not establish that a proposition is false.
:::

## 5. Try a larger public corpus

For a website, keep this tutorial as `example.qmd` and create
`more-sources.qmd` with this ordinary content:

```markdown
---
title: More public sources
---

::: {#conditional-result .local-ai-source data-source-label="A conditional result"}
If the stated assumptions hold, the declared conclusion follows. This
conditional statement does not establish that its assumptions hold.
:::
```

Use this small `_quarto.yml` in that two-page project, alongside your installed
extension:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
format: html
filters: [kai-prince-sfhea/local-ai-websites]
local-ai:
  corpus:
    pages: [example.html, more-sources.html]
```

Render the whole project and open its HTTP Preview. Open **Search a larger
selected public corpus** and choose **Load selected corpus**. Search for
`assumptions`, then choose **Show matching passages**.
Follow the original source and inspect its omitted-context counts. These are
exact source passages; no model wrote a summary. Choose **Use this page’s
sources** to return to this tutorial's smaller selection. For a local installation, use
`local-ai-websites` as the filter name.

## Next steps

Replace these synthetic excerpts with your own already-public material and
give each source a unique native ID. Keep one `.local-ai` panel per page.
The [README's advanced guidance](https://github.com/kai-prince-sfhea/local-ai-websites#customise-the-page)
covers project/page options, named-graph discovery, reviewed learning sources,
styling and optional visitor-confirmed browser-local models. To include another
page, first mark its public excerpts, then list its actual HTML output in
`source-pages` using the README's complete website YAML. The reader chooses
**Load selected page excerpts**; that action loads no model. With a compatible
Knowledge Graph Extraction installation, **Choose exact graph questions** offers
deterministic questions while keeping graph identities and coverage visible.

For a project already using both extensions, you can try smaller graph-detail
requests by merging this into its existing `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
knowledge-graph:
  delivery:
    mode: topics
```

Render Project and open its HTTP Preview. Choose an exact graph question and
run it. Watch the verified-part progress, or cancel and run again: complete
verified parts can be reused in this tab. The exact answer waits for all required
parts; a missing part does not become a claim that a concept or route is absent.
No model or author-written JavaScript is needed. Without topic delivery, the
same controls use the producer's ordinary complete graph file.

A model is an optional addition after this source-search workflow is working.
The default `proposal-format: cited-json` checks selected-excerpt quotations
before displaying an unreviewed proposal. Matching a quote does not show that
it supports a claim; a model can also return invalid JSON that is refused.
A complete response may be bare JSON or one whole `json` code fence; no author
configuration is needed. The original response is retained, the unchanged JSON
payload is checked, and the proposal remains unreviewed. Prose, partial responses
and invalid quotations are refused.
The README explains the explicit `plain-text` compatibility option. None of
these optional steps is required for this tutorial.

When you later enable a model, readers can separately choose **Reuse and keep**
to retain download checkpoints and resume when possible. Leaving it unchecked
keeps model bytes session-only. A complete model must still pass its byte-count
and SHA256 checks before use. The README explains the storage statuses and
**Delete saved model downloads**; no extra author script or YAML is required.

On a page with a compatible companion such as Interactive CV, the same ordinary
`.local-ai` panel supplies the model controls. Review, confirm and load the
language model here first; then explicitly request a proposal in the companion.
The companion can use only this page's ready engine and does not download or
start a model for you. Its deterministic extracts remain available when no
language model is ready. Source qualifications still need review.

When the project later declares a model manifest, a page can retain the other
project options while choosing its own graph scope. To keep this page limited
to source search, add this page option; it clears an inherited model manifest:

```yaml
local-ai:
  manifest: false
```

Use `local-ai: false` to turn the extension off entirely on a page. Project-wide
model preparation and advanced options are explained in the README.
